articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow falls, S&P 500 and Nasdaq retreat from records as Treasury yields hit 24-year high
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow falls, S&P 500 and Nasdaq retreat from records as Treasury yields hit 24-year high
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields came off their highs after a solid sale of 10-year notes. Earlier, the 10-year yield rose to its highest level in more than two decades.
The 10-year Treasury last traded around 3 basis points higher at 5.288%. Earlier in the session, it reached 5.35%, its highest level since 2002. The 30-year Treasury bond yield also traded below a 24-year high, at 5.67%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
The Treasury sold $39 billion of 10-year notes in an auction on Wednesday. According to BMO, the sale was "strong", with higher than average bidding from non-dealers.
Indirect bidders, which include global central banks, took 80.3% of the auction — above a 10-auction average of 72.4%. Direct bidders, scooped up 17.1% of the sale, just below an average of 18.3%. Dealers, meanwhile, bought just 2.5% of the notes offered, well below a 9.4% mean.
"The 24-year highs in rates brought out the buyers and resulted in a great auction," said Peter Boockvar, market strategist and author of The Boock Report.
Nonetheless, it still was the highest auction yield since 2000 at 5.3%.
This was the second of three Treasury Department sales this week. The government sold $58 billion in 3-year notes on Tuesday and is scheduled to sell $22 billion 30-year bonds on Thursday.
Treasury also will stage its latest buyback operation on Thursday, when it will be targeting maturities between 20 years and 30 years. The liquidity support operation will be at least $4 billion, or double the normal size. The last buyback in that range came to just over $4 billion.
Bonds have been selling off recently with investors concerned about inflation and rising energy prices. The 10-year has surged 60 basis points since the end of July, while U.S. crude prices have soared 20% in that time.
Selling pressure is also picking up overseas. The yield on the 10-year French bond surged 12 basis points to trade at 4.876%. The 10-year U.K. Gilt yield jumped 7 basis points to 5.447%.
Against that backdrop, FOMC meeting minutes were released, showing central bank officials expect to hike rates further — but gave no indication as to when .
"With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the summary of the Fed's September meeting stated.

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk
US President Donald Trump says he has a call set up with Vladimir Putin about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Russian officials say they are investigating the death of the 28-year-old employee and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic.
Trump told reporters on Wednesday evening he did not believe it was a bioweapon, adding "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so,"
"If you listen to them, it's under control," he said, referring to Russian authorities.
"We hope it is," he added. Reports emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation after the death.
Referring to China's initial response to the Covid pandemic, Trump said: "Well, China didn't say much, and Russia is not saying much either. But they do say they have it very much under control."
Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
Trump said the US was in "deep discussions" with Russia, but the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for more transparency from Russia, and requested further information on the lab tests on the individual who died.
"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, adding that the WHO was also seeking "verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause."
Ghebreyesus called on Russia to provide "timely, complete and transparent information" in order to clarify "conflicting reports" and help the WHO assess the potential public health risks.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information".
The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks".
This was a precautionary measure, it said, adding "the current risk level is low."
Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country.
Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has the stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency.
There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said.
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death .
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title_orig: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.title_zh: Western civilisation is 'at an inflection point' Rubio says in speech overloooking Acropolis
articles.content_orig:
Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.
"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.
"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."
His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.
The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.
In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.
"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."
The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.
The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.
Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."
In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.
Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.
"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.
The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.
"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.
In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.
The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."

A supertanker was recently chartered to sail from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, a source familiar told CNBC, as shipping costs soar globally due to the crisis in the Middle East.
The Alexandros was chartered by the trading firm Trafigura and is expected to load around Nov. 19, the source said. A normal rate for the route based on pre-war levels would be $7 million to $10 million.
The cost of the journey comes to $38 per barrel of oil assuming the tanker holds 2 million barrels. Shipping costs have exploded as the war in the Persian Gulf has led to a shortage of available tankers.
The Middle East producers are using a shuttle system to export oil through the Strait of Hormuz. A loaded tanker crosses the strait and then loads the oil onto another ship in the Gulf of Oman that takes the cargo to Asia. This system reduces the exposure to Iranian attack and has led to a rebound of crude exports through Hormuz. But it also requires a lot more ships to get the oil out of the Gulf.

articles.title_orig: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.title_zh: Piep Haus Projects Opens in North Andover with Arthur Henderson’s Hand-Hewn World of Folk Story
articles.content_orig:
A pie safe, a sausage rope, and a model of the universe are among the curious objects in Peasant’s Burlesque, curated by Stace Brandt.
Quick Bit by Monica Lynn Manoski
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
Installation view, Arthur Henderson, “Peasant’s Burlesque,” Piep Haus Projects, 2026. Courtesy of Piep House Projects. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
It was a subtly crisp afternoon with soft light casting long shadows on the curving roads of North Andover as I drove with the windows down to my destination, Piep Haus Projects (PHP), a new experimental pop-up art space hosted at the home of artist Leah Piepgras. I followed a series of hand-painted arrows up the driveway to the far end of a previously shag-carpeted house with the unmistakable vibes of a swingers pad, now transformed into a living space, artist studio, and exhibition room. On my way in, a young person with flowing dark hair snaked past me, weaving in and out of sculptures, down through the yard to the edge of Lake Cochichewick and back through to where I stood.
PHP’s inaugural show features works by Arthur Henderson, a MassArt graduate who now lives and works in “relative isolation” (other than the company of his wife and son) in the woods of Western Connecticut. “Peasant’s Burlesque ,” curated by Stace Brandt, brings together seventeen larger works—all completed since the start of the year—including fourteen sculptures, two woodblock prints, and a Portrait of the Artist at Work in ink on paper, with twenty-two small-scale sculptures housed separately in a cabinet.
Arthur Henderson, Big Red (front), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth with variable objects inside. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
A six-foot-wide wooden chandelier with snuffed candles drew me into the exhibition room in the far end of the house. Titled Model of the Universe from the outside looking in , it’s suspended from the vaulted ceiling with a charcoal-colored chain. The work’s seven distinct arms invite your eyes to return again and again to trace the irregular edges, which, although cut from plywood, have a hand-drawn quality.
​ Big Red (2026), a chestnut-colored pie cabinet with doors splayed, holds a curious accumulation of hand-carved items including a pipe, medicine cup, and a stack of Porterhouse steaks. Its plywood back bears chiseled hands spelling P-I-E-S-A-F-E in American Sign Language. Underneath its four legs, an ebony trap door gives a sense of dark mystery. I found myself imagining who or what is beneath it.
​A glowing ember box serves as a pedestal for a hand-hewn baguette and beer can. Custom-crafted box crates elevate other lovingly shaped objects, including Milkcrib , a four-walled resting place for an imagined gallon of milk, and Decoy (Skull in Repose) , a small sculpture resembling a bruised and tilted three-dimensional heart. Throughout the room things are placed casually—like how you might find a space left if someone weren’t expecting company. On my way out, I passed a staircase guarded by a string of sausage links and a sign marked “Champagne Room,” which made me smile and want to stay and snoop around.
(left) Detail view of objects inside Big Red including Steaks , 2026. (right) Big Red (back), 2026. Plywood, Bondo, paint cabinetry, and plinth. Courtesy of Piep Haus Projects.
The show exudes a whimsical, masculine energy, with each object serving as a breadcrumb to a larger narrative series the artist calls The Feast of the Butcher King . The objects in “Peasant’s Burlesque” are made from the perspective of the townsfolk who fall victim to the Butcher King in a retake on the folktale “Stone Soup.” The viewer enters a “set” where objects are contrived as offerings in exchange for the magic soup stone.
Brandt thoughtfully responded to the challenge of bringing Henderson’s purposely rough-hewn objects together with the newly renovated white cork-floored, multi-windowed project space. Henderson said, “What could’ve created a tension or competition instead feels very harmonious—a true conversation between the objects and their surroundings.”
​Arthur Henderson and Stace Brandt will be present with the work on Sunday, October 25, 2026, from 1:00 to 6:00 p.m. Between now and then, the space is open by appointment. Reach out to leah.piepgras@gmail.com for availability.

articles.title_zh: France suspends use of stun grenades to police student protests
articles.content_orig:
After a heavy-handed response to the student protests sweeping France , the government has changed tack.
It has banned police from using stun grenades after a student’s hand was blown off earlier in the week and there are promises to listen more to protesters’ demands.
But with hundreds of schools still facing blockade and calls for more protests, will it be enough?
“Empathy” and a little more “pedagogy” is what French President Emmanuel Macron demanded of police forces facing student protesters, said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, following a massive day of protests on Tuesday.
“The president recalled the necessity to maintain order, intervene each time there’s serious violence, all while asking us to act with the greatest proportionality,” Nunez told radio station RTL Wednesday, after an emergency ministerial meeting.
Nunez, a former chief of Paris’ police, said that he had ordered forces to refrain from using the type of stun grenade linked to a teenager losing his hand in protests on Monday.
“We don’t deal with a movement of highschoolers like we deal with a movement of adults,” Nunez said.
France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu told lawmakers Tuesday that high schools would replace lessons until the end of the week with a “period of internal democracy” to air grievances and discuss solutions.
While refuting any suggestion of police repression, Lecornu condemned violence on the margins of protests, which were mostly peaceful Tuesday, despite the dramatic scenes that dominated coverage.
In an address to the nation Wednesday, Lecornu said parliament would debate on November 12 a budget proposal that includes 64 billion euros ($71.6 billion) in funding for education, a slight increase from last year.
He also said the government has launched five initiatives to respond to students’ needs, including efforts to renovate school facilities, improve students’ schedules and provide more opportunities to express their concerns.
“We have a duty to listen to them. Taking young people seriously means supporting their engagement just as much as sharing the difficulties, but also the constraints, with them,” he said.
The proposal for discussion is a tried and tested tactic of Macron, who has historically favored attempts to integrate public debate into policy making. His government tried to calm the Yellow Vests protests with a similar listening campaign in 2019.
Meanwhile, 18 investigations into officers’ conduct during the protests have been opened by police internal investigators, Nunez said, adding they would examine the proportionality of police actions. Police forces “are there to protect the high schoolers,” he said.
On Wednesday, more than 500 educational institutions were due to be partially or fully closed because of blockades – a 41% decrease from Tuesday, according to the education ministry. That will leave 86% of schools open, the ministry added. According to the interior ministry, 488 people were detained around the high school protests Tuesday.
The student blockade actions on Wednesday were a fraction of the hundreds of thousands who marched with workers’ unions Tuesday in support of students across France. But it’s a sign of the rancor among students that protests are continuing day-to-day.
Student unions have called for a day of protests on October 17 and five major teaching unions said they would strike Thursday in solidarity with their students, with little sign that school blockades will halt in the meantime.
More teachers, smaller class sizes and buildings better adapted to the climate are the most common demands of high school protesters.
Student union leaders, who represent some of the young people protesting, have also called for a 10-billion-euro ($11.2-billion) investment in high school and university-level education.
A 10-point list of proposals drawn up by student unions included rethinking student workloads, ending a controversial university admissions system, ending police violence against students and creating more student accommodation.
Sabrine Kharbach, spokesperson of the Student Union federation of unionized students, told BFMTV that blockades would continue until their demands were met.
Anaïs Ella, spokesperson for Les Lycéens, a student association, told CNN that Lecornu didn’t address the demands laid out by student unions.
She said that some of the prime minister’s proposals – including filling teaching posts in exam-year classes – “was the basics of the education system.” She said that money would solve some of their demands but that a deeper reset in relations between the government and students was needed.
“We are the ones most directly affected by the national education system, yet we aren’t actually listened to,” she added.
Since the weekend, there have been concerted efforts among students to reject the violence that has marred protests.
Student Angelo Via, 19, who protested in the street Tuesday, told CNN there was a feeling of “powerlessness” in the face of violent police actions, despite many students protesting peacefully. He hopes the protests will bring about “radical change,” especially regarding education budgets.
There will be relief in France at the interior minister’s decision to ban one type of police grenade, as the injuries suffered by some teenage protesters has sparked widespread horror. But the proposal for time for debate has been met with skepticism in some quarters.
The main union for school directors, SNPDEN-UNSA, said that the single day set aside for discussions was insufficient to respond to problems in depth.
Nicolas Bonnet, national secretary of the union, told BFMTV that, “something other than a mere consultation period was required to get out of this crisis.”
France’s student protests highlight a debt crisis that could spill over to the rest of Europe
There are whispers in France of these protests transforming into another Yellow Vests movement, which was leaderless, nationwide and unified a broad church of grievances.
Mimicking the months-long violent protests – the longest in French history – that rocked Macron’s first term, students and journalists have already begun referring to the next day of protest set for Thursday as “Act IV.”

October 07, 2026 By Logan Culwell-Block
Other Bodies , a new solo play from Martin Moran , will make its world premiere Off-Broadway via Barrow Group, with performances beginning November 19 ahead of a November 23 opening night.
The work is the third in Moran's trilogy of solo works, following the 2004 Obie-winning The Tricky Part and 2013's Lucille Lortel Award-winning All the Rage . As with the earlier works, Seth Barrish is directing.
“For more than 20 years, these solo pieces have been a way for me to wrestle with questions I don’t know how to answer,” shares Moran in a statement. “ Other Bodies grew out of the pandemic, a moment when we were suddenly forced apart from one another, but it became an exploration of something much larger: how we live with difference, how we recognize experiences that aren’t our own, and how we find our way back to one another. I didn’t set out to write a trilogy, but returning to this form with Seth, and bringing this third piece to The Barrow Group, where The Tricky Part first began, feels like completing a circle.”
Moran's Broadway credits include roles in Spamalot , Cabaret , Titanic , Wicked , Big River , and Funny Girl , along with the Off-Broadway premiere of Floyd Collins .
Tickets are at BarrowGroup.org .

DES MOINES, Iowa (KCRG) - Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced Wednesday that she is suing surveillance video company ADI Global Distribution Inc.
The suit says ADI hid that the cameras manufacturers, Hikvision and Dahua, have close ties to the Chinese military.
The suit says both camera makers are on a list of foreign entities that pose a national security risk to the United States.
It says ADI has deceived Iowans for years by selling the products as their own brand.
It also accuses Hikvision and Dahua of deliberately engineering “backdoor” security vulnerabilities into their cameras that can be exploited for eavesdropping or criminal activity.
In a statement, Bird said “These China-made cameras are making Iowans’ private information — everything from where each room is in your home, who lives there, your routine, and even passwords — available to the Chinese government and military.”
This is the second lawsuit by Bird this week against China-aligned companies .

articles.title_orig: Fed officials see another hike coming, but no sign as to when, minutes show
articles.title_zh: Fed officials see another hike coming, but no sign as to when, minutes show
articles.content_orig: Federal Reserve officials expect they will raise interest rates again before the end of the year to head off inflation that has run above target for more than five years, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. But the meeting summary provided no indication of when specifically policymakers expected to raise benchmark rates – only that persistently higher prices and a stable labor market likely would lead to a second hike this year. The Fed next decides on rates on Oct. 28 and then again on Dec. 9. "With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond the current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the document stated. That position came with a note of caution. "Participants emphasized, however, that they approached each meeting with an open mind and decisions at future meetings would depend on incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks," the minutes said. Coming off the meeting, which featured tough inflation talk from Chairman Kevin Warsh during his subsequent news conference, markets started betting the Fed would follow the Sept. 16 hike with another move at the late October meeting. However, recent inflation data and comments from leading Fed officials indicate that at least for October, another increase is unlikely. The Fed's preferred gauge – the personal consumption expenditures price index – showed core inflation at 3% for August and headline at 3.4%. While both readings were still well north of the central bank's 2% target, they were considerably lower than expectations, benefiting in part from changes in the way some of the inputs are calculated. Discussion at the September meeting showed officials see risks that inflation will prove sticky, while the labor market is "close to maximum employment" and economic growth overall has picked up. The vote to raise the benchmark funds rate by a quarter percentage point was unanimous, despite prior indications that several key officials were reluctant to hike. "Many participants emphasized that a higher path for the target range would be prudent on risk-management grounds, providing insurance against inflation remaining persistently above target due to stronger-than-expected demand or further adverse supply shocks," the summary said. As a group, the Federal Open Market Committee indicated one more hike this year, then none in 2027. Of the 18 FOMC officials who submitted forecasts, 16 said they expected another increase. Warsh has not submitted a forecast since taking the position in May. During his news conference, he described the rate rise as removing "a dose of accommodation" from monetary policy, a remark that Wall Street analysts pored over and took to mean that additional increases could be on the way. But several other officials since then have stressed that the Fed doesn't need to rush, while inflation data has been at least a bit more encouraging even if short-term expectations have risen considerably. Market-based indicators for inflation are still elevated, and a fresh survey released Wednesday by the New York Fed showed consumer fears over rising prices in the next year are at their highest since May 2023. Treasury yields have been soaring as well, hitting levels not seen since 2002. Officials at the meeting discussed the rise in yields, attributing them to expectations for higher rates from the Fed as well as the build-out in artificial intelligence and solid economic growth. Staff economists also noted that some of the surge may have come from "uncertainty related to the U.S. Treasury's announcement and implementation of the buyback program." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August announced his department would ramp up its buybacks of already-issued long-dated debt. However, the move has had little impact on yields, which are around their highest levels since 2002.

articles.title_orig: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.title_zh: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.content_orig:
The Nova music festival memorial site on Oct. 07, 2026.
The world changed when Hamas attacked Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023 , catalyzing devastating conflict throughout the region . But within Israel, political sentiments have changed surprisingly little.
To some, the attack fulfilled long-term right-wing warnings that Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza would yield disaster; and the attack was incontrovertible proof that Palestinians will never live in peace with Israel.
Israeli left-wingers, for their part, have long held that a festering military rule over Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, and failure to reach peace, would inevitably lead to violent conflagration. For them, Oct. 7 only proved that they had been right all along.
The standoff raises crucial questions. In three years since Oct. 7, how has the attack changed Israeli society? And how will the answer affect upcoming elections in Israel?
To be sure, there have been cataclysmic changes in Israel, and the Middle East at large, since Oct. 7. The war in Gaza that began that day has become Israel’s longest war. A relatively stable ceasefire with Lebanon from 2006 to 2023 ended when Hezbollah, a Shi’a militia group, fired on Israel the day after Hamas’ attack; after multiple escalations since then, the current ceasefire is precarious. Israel and the U.S. have waged two full-blown wars with Iran, and the Middle East is still threatened by spin-off conflicts.
The losses Israelis suffered on Oct. 7 and since then have affected the country collectively and profoundly. For two years, many Israelis went from demonstration to demonstration demanding that their government prioritize a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages. Hundreds of thousands have spent the last three years in and out of active reserve duty.
Since 2023, Israel has seen record levels of emigration and growing international isolation. Sixty-one percent of Israelis told pollsters for the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) that the national mood is poor .
Moreover, the destruction of Palestinian life and society , still ongoing , will one day force a terrible reckoning within Israel.
What’s less visible, and more surprising, is what has stayed the same. Israelis’ attitudes towards Palestinians, occupation, and conflict have become more extreme. But I would argue that Israeli public opinion today says much more about how Israel had changed prior to Oct. 7. The change in national attitudes since that fateful day has been moderate and consistent with what came before.
In December 2022, almost a year before Oct. 7, support for peace through a two-state solution hit a historic low. In the joint Palestinian-Israeli survey I conduct together with colleagues at Tel Aviv University and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, support stood at 39% of Israelis that year—the lowest since the 1990s. Among Jewish respondents, just 34% supported a two-state solution, and 37% believed Israel should permanently annex the West Bank while Palestinians would have limited rights.
When we conducted the study again in mid-2024, Jews were twice as likely to support a single, Israeli-dominated unequal state as they were to support two states.
Palestinian attitudes in 2022 were similar. Just one-third supported two states. Both sides showed a mirror-image majority who distrusted the other. In surveys by the IDI from that same time, 59% of Jewish Israelis defined themselves as right-wing; just 12% said they were left-wing.
What changed after Oct. 7? This July, the Tel Aviv University Peace Index survey found that support for two states stood at 31%, an eight-point decline in the four years since 2022. Now, IDI surveys find that just over 60% of Israeli Jews describe themselves as right-wing, just a few points higher than late 2022.
Israel has changed, but this change began years before Oct. 7 2023. In 2010 , no fewer than 71% of Israelis supported a two-state solution in the joint surveys. The years that followed were plagued by stagnation and dissipation of any peace process, regular wars with Hamas, and a heavily nationalist government in Israel. It stands to reason that these phenomena pushed Israeli society further to the right. Support for the two-state solution eroded slowly, then rapidly by the end of the decade.
That shift was self-reinforcing: the more right-wing Israelis became (primarily the Jewish population), the more elected leaders took ever-more radical positions such as supporting settlement expansion and de facto annexation in the West Bank. In 2019, Prime Minister Netanyahu began referring to extending sovereignty over parts of the West Bank, or de jure annexation . The current government accelerated those processes drastically.
Study after study shows that Arab citizens of Israel have remained the strongest supporters of peace, before and after the current wars. But with Jewish Israeli and Palestinian attitudes so dismal in the years before Oct. 7, the chances of resurgent violence almost seemed inevitable.
In other words, most Israelis did not radically transform their worldview after Oct. 7. In fact, hardline political trends were among the many factors contributing to the terrible escalation to begin with.
Another thing that hasn’t changed in Israel during the last three years of war: hopes for peace. The number of Israeli Jews who self-describe as left-wing has barely shifted. In a May survey for the Institute for National Security Studies, about 20% of the total population, Jews and Arabs, define themselves as left-wing, and a similar share typically say they are centrist. These groups embrace a commitment to democracy, liberal values, separation of religion and state, and reject the religious fundamentalism of the current government.
The left remains committed to peace via diplomacy and Palestinian self-determination. In a mid-2025 survey I conducted for a peace organization called A Land for All, where I am also an active member, the large majority of self-defined left-wing Israelis, and nearly half of centrists, supported a basic two-state solution.
Do peace attitudes even matter, when there is no peace process? That may be theoretical for now, but elections aren’t. Israelis will be voting on Oct. 27. Polls show the voters deeply divided , just as they were in the elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is not doing well. Nearly all polls show his coalition parties well below their actual result in 2022. And most mainstream polls show a consistent majority for today’s opposition parties.
At first glance, these shifts might seem antithetical. Aren’t these ideological and electoral trends moving in contradictory directions: more right-wing, but a majority against the current government?
It turns out that even the Israeli electoral contradiction is not new. During the five elections from 2019 through 2022, a majority of Israelis were right-wing and voted for right-wing parties. But to form a coalition, some of those parties no longer supported Netanyahu and refused to join a coalition under his leadership. Netanyahu therefore commanded only about half the seats in parliament following four of these cycles. Neither side had a clear or firm coalition majority, and the country was thrown into electoral turmoil five times over.
But if all mainstream polls show the anti-Netanyahu parties winning, including right-wing opposition parties, shouldn’t that mean a decisive outcome against him this time? Not quite: no poll shows Israel’s Jewish, Zionist parties reaching a majority in October.
And in Israel’s right-wing, populist discourse, the main opposition party leaders opposed to Netanyahu now, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, with similar statements from frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot , insist that parties representing Arab citizens must not be part of a coalition after Oct. 7. Microsoft’s high-end AI mini PC for developers starts shipping in November.﻿
Microsoft’s Nvidia-powered Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder now and is slated to ship in November for just about $6,000. It’s pricier than the DGX Spark mini PC Nvidia launched last year, but PC prices have been climbing due to shortages of RAM and other components .
The Dev Box’s flat, 3D-printed anodized aluminum chassis doubles as a heatsink and resembles the top vents on an Xbox Series X. It was introduced alongside the new Surface Laptop Ultra and runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform and 128GB of unified memory. With that much memory, along with a 100-watt thermal envelope and Nvidia’s Tensor cores, you could probably get an impressive gaming experience on the Dev Box. articles.title_orig: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

Doc is one of only two B-29s still flying today. More than 1,600 were built in Wichita during the war.
It is joined by a P-51 Mustang. Those are rare too. Only about 150 of them are still around.
Visitors got a chance to see the aircraft up close and learn about the crews who designed, built and flew them.
“It’s a pretty special opportunity...really makes the history jump off the page,” Josh Wells said.
Wells said the event also helps younger generations understand an important piece of history.

articles.title_zh: Asia Focus: Expanding Global Reach, World's Most Populous Continent Continues To Flourish
articles.content_orig:
Get Pollstar News and more delivered right to your inbox with Pollstar Daily Pulse.
By signing up, you agree to Pollstar’s Privacy Policy and Terms of Use
The Asian touring market continues to thrive, with promoters and venues reaping the rewards of artists both homegrown and international presenting top-notch concert productions at home and abroad, with new partnerships and long-lasting relationships behind the scenes meaning the traffic is both inbound as well as exported to the rest of the world.
The dominance of K-pop in the region, anchored by activity in Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Indonesia and Dubai, continues. The top four touring acts, as reported to Pollstar (see page 162), were K-pop bands, with SEVENTEEN showing the way with a gross of $97,394,005. TWICE grossed $76,176,781 and TOMORROW X TOGETHER did $53,035,381. Ranked No. 4, Korean powerhouse BTS grossed $49,069,994 in Asia as part of its mammoth “ARIRANG” world tour, which was No. 1 on Pollstar ’s Q3 chart. Those shows were the chart-topping boy band’s first in nearly four years due to military service.
Western acts were busy as well, with Lady Gaga leading the charge ($44,379,794 grossed), fifth overall in the territory, and Travis Scott was close behind ($37,922,441). Just to reinforce the Asian presence in the home region, G.E.M. came in seventh ($31,725,779), BLACKPINK is eighth ($29,193,966 grossed) and ENHYPEN nabbed the ninth spot ($21,562,532 grossed).
The key players in the region who Pollstar talked to were uniformly enthusiastic about business. HYBE was the leading promoter in the region with $247,965,087 in gross revenue. HYBE 360 President Yoojin Oh (Impact Honoree, see page 176), who oversees the company’s concert business, says, “Over the past year, HYBE artists’ global tours have continued to expand not only in scale but also in the breadth of markets they reach.”
Japan’s presence as the longtime leader in the Asian music industry remained strong. Three of the top five promotion agencies were Japanese and the country held six of the top 10 spots. The biggest player in the nation was Creativeman Productions, with $103,665,840 in gross revenue, third overall in Pollstar ’s Asia chart. Naoki Shimizu, president of the promoter behind the long-running Summer Sonic festival, notes, “The live music market has bounced back from the pandemic and is expanding even more than before.” Of Japan in particular, he says, “The breadth of the entertainment landscape is a key factor. There is a capacity to turn anything — whether local acts, Asian artists, Western music, anime, or voice actors — into a major live concert market.” In second place for promoters was Live Nation with $209,803,871 in gross revenue reported.
Dennis Argenzia, president of global touring, Asia-Pacific at Live Nation, has observed a shift in enthusiasm from artists. “Asia is at a really exciting point in its evolution as a live music market,” Argenzia says. “For many years, we had to convince artists and their teams to come to Asia — today, the conversation is very different. Artists want to perform here because they see the growth in demand and the opportunity to build deeper connections with fans across the region.”
Hong Kong appears as a microcosm of the expanding Asia market. The 50,000- capacity Kai Tak Stadium is a crucial venue for all of Asia. Kath Wong, senior manager at the firm that runs the stadium, emphasizes the outsized role K-pop plays in Asia touring and Hong Kong’s place in the market, with concert highlights from BLACKPINK and SEVENTEEN at Kai Tak Stadium.
“Each show serves as a milestone not only for Kai Tak Sports Park, but for Hong Kong as a whole,” Wong says. “It demonstrated that the stadium could host some of the world’s biggest touring artists and deliver complex international production to the standard expected by the artist, promoter and production teams.”
She expands on the environment, with Kai Tak Sports Park including both the 50,000-seat stadium with a retractable roof and the indoor Kai Tak Arena, which can accommodate 10,000 people and has 80% retractable seating.
Irene Chan, CEO of AsiaWorld-Expo, which operates the 14,000-cap arena of the same name in Hong Kong (the third biggest in Asia), is extremely upbeat on the business in 2026: “Audiences increasingly seek destination events that combine music, culture, fashion, art, retail, food and technology—driving the global trend of ‘festivalisation’ and creating new revenue and partnership opportunities beyond ticket sales.”
Global promoter AEG Presents, based in the U.S., is also focused on the region. Adam Wilkes, president and CEO of AEG Presents Europe and Asia-Pacific, who has worked in the Asian touring market for decades, offers a comprehensive overview.
“Asia is already a core part of the global touring ecosystem, and its significance will only grow,” he says. “International artists are reaching more markets, supported by a wave of world-class venues – both newly opened and under construction. The regional touring industry is also becoming more sophisticated, allowing artists to build meaningful careers across multiple countries rather than only at home.”
He adds that the world environment has changed, catapulting Asia to a new position. “Crucially, the traffic now moves both ways,” he says. “K-pop led the way, but Japanese, Chinese and Indian artists are increasingly finding audiences and performing at the highest level around the world. More inbound touring, better infrastructure and a growing pipeline of internationally successful Asian talent make the potential enormous.”
In Japan, Shimizu reflects on Creativeman’s successes but also looks forward.
“After Summer Sonic, the biggest tour of the year for us would be Iron Maiden,” he says of the globally renowned heavy metal pioneers. Other rock bands continue to show strength in the market. “Last year, it was Green Day, and Radiohead is coming up next year. It is a joy, after such a long career, to have tours every year by bands I’ve promoted for over two decades.”
The company is set to expand its dominant network even further. Shimizu explains, “Creativeman recently entered into a strategic partnership with AEG. In the past, artists like Taylor Swift, Justin Bieber and Ariana Grande have started out working with Creativeman for their Japan shows, only to move on to global tours handled by others. Now, however, we have a setting where we can continue working with them throughout that process. Furthermore, Creativeman’s 36 year-career will undoubtedly bring added value to AEG.”
Kaori Hayashi, president of Live Nation H.I.P. (Hayashi International Promotions), notes the promoter is set for a banner year. “We are seeing strong demand for live entertainment in Japan. More artists are touring, more live events are taking place, and more fans are attending these events. Bruno Mars’ 12-show dome tour in January 2027 will be the largest tour ever undertaken by an international artist in Japan. It will span six cities across the country – from Osaka to Nagoya – reflecting the depth of demand for international artists well beyond Tokyo, and is another indication of the scale of opportunity in this market.”
The 37,000-cap GMO Arena Saitama (formerly Saitama Super Arena), one of Japan’s biggest arenas and the second largest in Asia, has been closed for a major renovation since January. Operations will resume in April 2027, and Yutaka Minagawa, MD of the arena, tells Pollstar they have already secured a number of major international artist performances.
“Japan’s music market continues to benefit from strong and stable demand for domestic artists, particularly within the J-Pop genre,” Minagawa says. “In addition to J-Pop, K-Pop enjoys enduring popularity, while major international artists continue to include Japan as part of their world tours. This creates a highly diverse live entertainment ecosystem where multiple genres can successfully coexist.”

articles.title_zh: Paxton’s latest audio leak is making things tough for national Republicans
articles.content_orig:
by RAY LEWIS | The National News Desk
HUNT VALLEY, Md. (TNND) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the reeling Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, is blaming his so-far poor performance on factors beyond his control.
Paxton has trailed his Democratic opponent in most polls over the past few months as he struggles to attract donors wary of his legal baggage and attachment to the GOP's unpopular governance. He was charged with fraud in a since-dropped case and impeached by state Republicans, all the while defending the Trump administration's legally dubious dealings.
He told a group of donors and lobbyists at a recent closed-door event that the Iran war, and its subsequent effect on fuel prices, is more to blame for his campaign issues.
"It's the war, it's the gas prices, it's diesel," he said in an audio clip published by Axios Wednesday. "When it's over $6 a gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch. So I'd say that's probably the biggest problem."
The average price for a gallon of diesel in Texas is $5.72, according to AAA data, but rates in many other states are well above $6. Many Texans are upset over fuel costs, but Paxton's legal problems also present a challenging obstacle on his road to the Senate.
Eighty-five percent of voters told The New York Times and Siena University last month they have heard of the attorney general's controversies, and 45 percent of that group said they'll consider those issues at the polls.
Paxton's spent valuable time defending himself against attacks by state Representative James Talarico, who's leaned heavily on an anti-corruption platform.
"You shouldn't believe anything a politician says, whether it's me or Ken Paxton. You should look at what we've done," Talarico said in a Fox News interview last month. "And if you look at Ken Paxton's history, he has spent his entire career enriching himself on the public's dime. I'll put my record up against Ken Paxton's every day of the week."
The National News Desk requested comment from the attorney general but hasn't received a response.
He's focused on Talarico's positions on cultural issues, which helped Republicans take control of the Senate, House and White House two years ago. The Democrat, Paxton says, is too far left for Texas's reliably red electorate.
"Texas is NOT California. James Talarico is the most radical Senate candidate our state has ever seen," Paxton said in a September call for donations. "Help us stop him before National Democrats turn Texas blue."

articles.title_orig: Modelo owner Constellation is getting creative to bring back beer drinkers as overall demand weakens
articles.title_zh: Modelo owner Constellation is getting creative to bring back beer drinkers as overall demand weakens
articles.content_orig:
Constellation Brands beat quarterly earnings and revenue expectations as its beer brands gained market share, but continued consumer caution tempered results.
As it navigates high food and fuel prices and choosy shoppers, Constellation is turning to special occasions and diversification to help drive sales.
The maker of Modelo Especial, Corona and Pacifico on Tuesday reported fiscal second-quarter adjusted earnings of $3.74 per share on $2.63 billion in revenue, ahead of Wall Street estimates of $3.56 and $2.54 billion, respectively.
Beer revenue rose 5% to roughly $2.47 billion, while beer shipments increased 5.5%. However, the company said beer depletions, a measure of sales from distributors to retailers and other customers, declined slightly during the quarter, indicating consumer demand was softer than shipment growth suggests.
"We have spent much of the first half rebuilding distributor inventory levels," said Constellation Brands CEO Nicholas Fink on the company's earnings call on Wednesday. "While there is always going to be month-to-month variability, September depletions are trending in the right direction."
The broader backdrop remains challenging for beer sellers. U.S. beer sales fell 1.8% year over year in the two weeks ended Sept. 19, according to Nielsen's latest data.
Still, Fink said September beer depletions improved even beyond the benefit of a later Labor Day, and that the recovery was broad-based across channels. He said consumers were "across the board" engaging in the category.
Some analysts said the results indicated elevated gas prices have dampened Constellation's performance.
“Progress [for Constellation] had accelerated to start 2026, but has been derailed by higher fuel costs,” Roth Capital analyst Bill Kirk wrote, though he said Constellation continues to deliver against its fiscal 2027 plan. Kirk has a buy rating and $209 price target on the stock, compared with the roughly $116 a share price as of Wednesday.
Fink said Constellation saw particular strength in club stores, which have benefited as cash-strapped shoppers seek deals on fuel and groceries. The company is also working to better tailor its product and pack sizes across channels, as consumers make different choices depending on where they are shopping, and for what occasion.
That focus on events also extends to younger drinkers. Fink said consumers are increasingly buying beer for specific moments, rather than treating it as a default purchase, and Constellation is leaning into sports, music, beach activations and other occasions to drive sales.
The company's pricing strategy reflects consumer caution around spending.
Chief Financial Officer Garth Hankinson said Constellation has been selective with price increases, keeping them at the low end of its usual range given the "macroeconomic backdrop and the impact that that's having on our consumer." Hankinson said it is "much more cost-effective to retain your consumers than it is to try to regain your consumers."
That price sensitivity is especially important for Constellation, given its reliance on Hispanic shoppers. About 40% of spending on Constellation's beer comes from Hispanic consumers, compared with roughly 15% for the overall beer category, according to company data.
That cohort has faced more economic concerns , including pressure from the labor market and household finances in part fueled by President Donald Trump's policy of mass deportation. Constellation has previously said that beer demand has been weaker in areas with larger Hispanic populations, although it has also pointed to improving trends in some markets.
Constellation is also moving beyond its core beer business. The company announced Tuesday that it would acquire SpikedAde , a spirit-based ready-to-drink beverage brand, for $75 million up front, with up to another $278 million in potential payments tied to future performance.
The deal gives Constellation a foothold in a new segment that has drawn more interest from consumers. Fink said the company aims to "remain relevant to our consumers and to our customers," adding that distributors have urged Constellation to get into growing categories beyond beer.
Some analysts approved of the move.
"We consider the acquisition attractive, giving [Constellation] exposure to the fast-growing RTD subcategory," said Piper Sandler analyst Michael Lavery, who also noted that Stateside Vodka's competing Super Lyte brand has also had "a very strong start" on the East Coast.
Lavery has a neutral rating and $161 price target on Constellation's stock.
While Fink said beer will remain the company's primary source of value creation, he called SpikedAde a "long, wide-open runway" for Constellation's brand-building and distribution capabilities.
According to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, sales of premixed cocktails including spirits-based RTDs grew 16.4% in 2025 to $3.8 billion, making them the spirits industry's strongest growth category.
Correction: Constellation reported earnings Tuesday and held its conference call Wednesday. A previous version misstated those dates.

This blog has now closed. Read below for a look at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany plans to buy four more Meko A-200 frigates from TKMS for about €5.6 million   ($6.3 billion), the Reuters news agency reported on Tuesday, citing a Finance Ministry document.
The country's parliamentary budget committee is expected to approve the purchase on Thursday, with the construction due to be finalized by 2035, as per Finance Ministry documents seen by Reuters.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius had cancelled a rival F126  frigate project with Dutch company Damen , over delays and cost overruns.
Germany’s far-right AfD party took a significant step toward exercising political power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
One month after winning 44% of the regional vote, the party secured the presidency of the state parliament, with Tobias Rausch elected as speaker of the house.
What does this moment mean for Germany? DW reports from Magdeburg.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Parliamentarians in Saxony-Anhalt have also voted for AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider to be one of the deputy speakers in the chamber.
This follows Tobias Rausch of the right-wing populist AfD being voted into the speaker's role earlier on Tuesday.
Tillschneider received 44 votes in favor in Tuesday's session, while 38 parliamentarians opposed his appointment. Nobody abstained from the vote, which was by secret ballot. The AfD has 39 seats in the chamber.
Lawmakers decided to elect three deputy speakers in total, with elections for the others expected to follow later.
Tillschneider, aged 48, is the deputy chair of the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group. He's an AfD veteran, having joined the party in 2013 soon after it was founded.
Tillschneider is a member of the identitarian movement, and was a member of the two AfD fringe groups — the so-called Flügel (wing) and its "Patriotic Platform" — that have since been formally disbanded. He also had close ties to the Pegida and Legida groups that organized anti-migrant protests in eastern Germany.
As well as his strong views on Islam and migration, Tillschneider is also known for his ties to Vladimir Putin's Russia. He was one of three AfD parliamentarians to visit Russia in September 2022, barely six months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine , in a visit that AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel rapidly disowned as a "private trip" and "not productive."
Since 2023, Tillschneider has written a monthly column for the Vedomosti newspaper in Russia. He attended the 73rd birthday celebrations for Putin at the Russian Embassy in Berlin last October.
The outgoing premier of Saxony-Anhalt says he can't explain where an additional four votes backing the AfD's Tobias Rausch as the state's new parliamentary speaker came from.
In a first for the far-right party, 35-year-old Rausch was elected to the post on Tuesday with the help of the populist BSW party (see entry below).
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group leadership had recommended that its 15 lawmakers in the state parliament abstain from voting.
But CDU regional leader and current state Premier Sven Schulze said it had become clear by this morning that not all the party's lawmakers planned to do so.
Some indicated that they planned to vote "no," Schulze said in comments to the German press agency DPA. "But none of us said we would vote 'yes,'" he added. "Not a single one."
Rausch was elected with 48 votes in favor and 29 against from 82 eligible votes in the secret ballot. There were five abstentions.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, meaning Rausch also got backing from members of other parties besides the AfD and BSW.
The center-left Social Democrats demanded answers, with the party's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, calling for the CDU to "immediately clarify who from within its ranks may have considered this disastrous decision to be right."
Klüssendorf also criticized the BSW for supporting Rausch's election.
"The BSW has made a conscious decision to elect, for the first time since 1945, a politician from a far-right party to the leadership of a German parliament," Klüssendorf told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
In addition to the CDU, the Social Democrats and the BSW, the Left party and the Greens are also represented in the state's parliament. Except for the BSW, the other parties have refused to work with the AfD, but some combination of them cast a secret vote for Rausch.
The Volksbank Köln Bonn in western Germany has agreed to part ways with a board member, Jürgen Neutgens, after a scandal over a loan he authorized to Cologne 's large brothel, Pascha.
It made the announcement on Tuesday, several months after placing Neutgens on leave and commissioning an independent law firm to investigate the transaction for potential wrongdoing.
"The investigation ... found no indications of financial irregularities or actions contravening obligations in the loan processes or the business relationship," the bank said in a press release . "Nevertheless the past weeks have weighed considerably on everyone involved."
Against this backdrop, the bank said the parties involved had mutually concluded that "a trusting and candid cooperation for the future can no longer be continued on the appropriate foundation."
It said both sides had agreed to confidentiality on the further details and terms, and thanked Neutgens for his service and wished him well for the future.
The loan was issued amid the restrictions of the COVID pandemic, which took a severe toll on the sex industry in Germany and led to the Pascha brothel in Cologne filing for insolvency and then changing ownership .
A family from China, or more specifically the autonomous casino-rich region of Macao, bought the business. But they needed a bridging loan of around €5 million (roughly $5.6 million at today's exchange rates) to cover part of the purchase price when their funds were held up in Hong Kong.
A typical German Christmas speciality intended as a gift for Pope Leo XIV was driven to Rome in an official vehicle from the state of Saxony after it was deemed unsuitable for air transport, officials revealed on Tuesday.
The 4-kilogram (8.8-pound) cake, a so-called stollen, which was made in the Ore Mountains in eastern Germany, was taken by Saxon Premier Michael Kretschmer to the Vatican for a private audience at the end of September.
The cake was reportedly too large to be taken into the cabin and too fragile to be placed in the aircraft hold, the officials said.
No information was provided on the cost by the officials at the Saxon State Chancellery.
The vehicle also transported other presents and documents.
The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt , Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) , Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker.
The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said.
"We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added.
Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle."
Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state."
The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it.

articles.title_orig: Nissan UK launches first ‘real-world’ driverless pilot
articles.title_zh: Nissan UK launches first ‘real-world’ driverless pilot
articles.content_orig:
Part of a government-funded research project that originated at the University of Warwick, it aims to deploy an autonomous mobility service across the U.K.
Nissan U.K.’s business unit will bring autonomous driving services to the university city of Cambridge and test its latest technology in an urban enviorment and create a blueprint to launch in other communities.
The plans are part of a government-funded research project backed by Nissan that launched in September 2023 at the University of Warwick with the goal of deploying an autonomous mobility service across the U.K.
The pilot trial, dubbed “ADventure,” will be coordinated between the automaker, local authorities, commuters and residents, the company said in its Sept. 28 release .
Using a specially adapted 2022 Nissan Leaf electric vehicle , the project hopes to focus on how future AD technology “can create social value, improve accessibility and address local transport challenges,” Nissan said.
The automaker used the common example of elderly people in the U.K. having to travel to a medical appointment when they do not drive themselves.
Nissan will draw on more than a decade of research by its engineers at the Nissan Technical Center Europe, which will lead the autonomous mobility project.
By choosing the driving environment in Cambridge for the automaker’s first real-world trial, Nissan aims to create a blueprint that it can refine and replicate across the U.K.
“This project is an important step for autonomous mobility in the UK,” said David Moss, SVP research and development for Nissan vehicles across the Africa, Middle East, India, Europe and Oceania regions. “With UK Government backing, it will take autonomous vehicle research beyond central London and into another city, helping us understand how these services can work for different communities and real-life journeys.”
“By developing and applying Nissan’s in-house expertise, combined with the wider knowledge from our partners, we can delve further into how self-driving vehicles can improve connectivity, accessibility and quality of everyday life,” Moss added.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.content_orig:
Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed.
Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian revealed in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.
The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy”.
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30% – though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
after newsletter promotion
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall , this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

articles.title_orig: Students at Lincoln University, an HBCU, Sue Missouri for $549 Million, Citing Funding Disparities
articles.title_zh: Students at Lincoln University, an HBCU, Sue Missouri for $549 Million, Citing Funding Disparities
articles.content_orig:
Lincoln University students and alumni filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the state of Missouri on Wednesday, alleging decades of unequal funding between it and the University of Missouri.
The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri and is the first case brought by the 1890 Project challenging a state allegedly failing to appropriately fund an 1890 land-grant university, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers.
The 1890 Project monitors promises made in the federal government's second Morrill Act in 1890, which aimed to ensure historically Black universities were equitably funded as certain white universities had been through the original 1862 Morrill Act.
These land-grant institutions were supposed to be provided funding for programs to strengthen research, extension and teaching, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture .
The New York Times reported that between 1987 and 2020 , federal officials found Missouri appropriated $361.6 million less to Lincoln on a per-student basis than to the University of Missouri.
The students and alumni are seeking a court-ordered remedy to combat the alleged disparity and permanently require that Missouri fully match Lincoln's federal land-grant funding.
They also allege that the funding disparity stems from the University of Missouri being founded in 1839 for white students and Lincoln University being separately designated as a land-grant institution in 1890 for Black students.
The University of Missouri is an 1862 land-grant university , established under different legislation than the 1890 land-grant universities.
